Gboard Privacy and Diagnostic Flags: What to Avoid Enabling

Identify flags that may affect diagnostic data, audio history and training caches, and learn how to evaluate privacy implications.

What you should know

A diagnostic flag name is not a privacy guarantee. Avoid collecting sensitive typing or speech data without an explicit reason.

Evidence standard: these are real catalog identifiers, but their effects can be inferred, version-specific, or gated. Check the confidence and APK notes before changing settings.

Logging and feature behavior aren't interchangeable

enable_internal_speech_enhancement_pii_logging indicates logging connected to speech-enhancement internals, not a normal feature to enable casually. enable_save_audio_history_to_file suggests persistence of audio-related data. enable_logging_for_emoji_search_query likewise concerns traces that could reveal what was typed or searched. These are especially poor candidates for blanket 'recommended tweaks' lists.

Local caches have tradeoffs

Gboard includes references to user-feature caches, training caches and locally aggregated metrics. A flag's presence does not tell us the exact retention period, where data is stored, whether encryption is used or which diagnostic endpoint might receive a report. Even an 'on-device' name does not certify the absence of all network activity.

Use normal privacy controls

Prefer supported Gboard privacy and personalization settings, avoid enabling PII/audio logging, and review permissions with Android settings when investigating behavior. If you need evidence for the Atlas, inspect code paths in an APK or use synthetic test inputs. Don't upload a private real-world cache or speech recording just to decipher a flag.

Frequently asked questions

Does disabling a logging flag stop all telemetry?

No. One identifier is not a complete audit of every diagnostics and network path.

Is exporting the UFC cache safe?

Its exported fields and destination are unverified. Treat the data as potentially sensitive.

  • Google Gboard — troubleshoot personalization
  • Google Search Central — people-first sources and transparency

Gboard Key Correction and Touch Accuracy: What the Flags Mean

Explore Gboard key-correction thresholds, personalized touch offsets and the research behind mistap handling.

What you should know

Typing accuracy depends on how the decoder interprets touch positions, not merely the visual size of the keyboard.

Evidence standard: these are real catalog identifiers, but their effects can be inferred, version-specific, or gated. Check the confidence and APK notes before changing settings.

Where KC differs from AC

Key correction (KC) is related to interpreting taps and neighboring-key errors before or alongside word decoding. Autocorrection (AC) instead concerns word replacements. An enable_kc_threshold flag points to a possible control in this process, but its numeric semantics and effects aren't independently measured by the Atlas.

What research can actually establish

Google's published spatial-model personalization work describes adapting virtual-key centers and learned touch behavior. It found measurable but modest improvements in speed and decoder accuracy across real typing. That paper supports the overall concept, not the exact effect of any particular enable_ufc_for_offset toggle extracted from a later APK.

Test the right failure mode

If you hit an adjacent letter by accident, compare words corrected from the same mistap patterns. Keep layout size and typing posture constant. Changing keyboard height while testing a key-correction flag creates a confound; it changes where your fingers land. Prefer repeated phrases and save the original configuration.

Frequently asked questions

Does offset refer to spacing between keys?

In this context, the plausible meaning is learned touch displacement relative to key centers, not a promise of physical key movement.

Can a flag fix a broken touchscreen?

No. Input hardware, scaling, autocorrection and learned touch models are different layers.

Gboard Typing Lag and Battery: What Flags Can Actually Tell You

Separate measurable Gboard responsiveness from unsupported 'speed boost' flag claims and apply safer troubleshooting first.

What you should know

There is no verified magic speed-up flag in this catalog; benchmark a reproducible problem before changing model or cache settings.

Evidence standard: these are real catalog identifiers, but their effects can be inferred, version-specific, or gated. Check the confidence and APK notes before changing settings.

Find the symptom before changing anything

A delay opening the keyboard, a missed keypress, slow suggestion refresh and a model download are different problems. Measure which one occurs and in which app. Google recommends ordinary cache and personalization troubleshooting for lag, but clearing app storage resets preferences; don't start there if you need to preserve learned settings.

What performance-looking flags actually mean

enable_ufc_for_speed refers to typing-speed information in User Feature Cache; it is not demonstrated to speed up Gboard. enable_sqlite_release_memory suggests a database memory-release path, not a proven lower RAM footprint. disable_nwp_result_cache could even remove a cache that normally avoids repeated work. Reading the words of a flag as a measured optimization is a common mistake.

Run a useful before-and-after test

Compare startup latency after a cold keyboard activation and suggestion latency during a fixed typing sequence. Record Gboard version, battery mode, model-download status and keyboard language. Don't change cache, model and UI animation flags at once. If a change only modifies visuals, don't advertise it as a battery-saving breakthrough without current draw measurements.

Frequently asked questions

Which flag should I turn on for less lag?

None has a verified universal performance improvement in this reference. Start by identifying the specific lag.

Can a cache flag reduce memory and make performance worse?

Yes, in principle: removing cached results can trade memory consumption for repeat computation. This specific flag's effect is not measured.

  • Spatial model personalization in Gboard

Gboard UFC Flags: User Feature Cache, Touch Offsets and Speed

Read the APK evidence identifying UFC as User Feature Cache, and distinguish cached typing information from a supposed speed boost.

What you should know

UFC maps to User Feature Cache in the inspected GboardWu APK; the speed flag is not a general performance accelerator.

Evidence standard: these are real catalog identifiers, but their effects can be inferred, version-specific, or gated. Check the confidence and APK notes before changing settings.

What the APK actually calls UFC

Read-only analysis of GboardWu 18.5.4 identified package paths including com/google/android/libraries/inputmethod/userfeaturecache/guarder/UfcGuarder and UfcMetricsProcessorModule. These class names strongly support User Feature Cache as the expansion. They do not disclose every stored field or the persistence and export policy.

Interpret the three visible controls

enable_ufc_for_offset plausibly allows the decoder to use learned touch offsets. enable_ufc_for_speed plausibly uses a learned typing-speed signal rather than increasing processor speed. enable_export_ufc suggests an export path, but its destination and field contents are unverified. These are interpretations grounded in code context; individual runtime call-site outcomes have not been proven.

What not to infer

A paper on personalized keyboard geometry describes offset learning and measured decoder improvements, but it is not evidence that flipping the UFC switches yields those gains. An export toggle deserves caution because cached typing-related statistics can be sensitive. Avoid enabling diagnostics or dumping personal data simply to answer a curiosity.

Frequently asked questions

Does UFC make Gboard faster?

It may provide typing-speed information; the examined flag does not establish a performance boost.

What is in the UFC export?

The precise exported fields and destination are not documented by the evidence currently available to the Atlas.

Gboard V2 KLP Loader Explained From Real APK Bytecode

Investigate disable_load_v2_klp, the real default and the LatinIme call site—without inventing a legacy loader or layout-package expansion.

What you should know

The real flag name is disable_load_v2_klp. It is read by LatinIme and changes internal configuration when true; a forced V1 fallback is not proven.

Evidence standard: these are real catalog identifiers, but their effects can be inferred, version-specific, or gated. Check the confidence and APK notes before changing settings.

The exact declaration

In the inspected GboardWu 18.5.4.993608717 arm64 APK, classes.dex registers disable_load_v2_klp as a boolean with a declared false default. This is the APK's hardcoded declaration, not necessarily the server-overridden value. The full disable_ prefix is essential: descriptions that say 'Load V2 KLP' obscure the switch's direction.

The consumer is real

In classes5.dex, com.google.android.apps.inputmethod.libs.latin5.LatinIme.O() reads the flag and, when true, sets an internal option bit 0x8 and a Boolean field on a generated configuration object. The same routine consumes lazy_load_klp_sections, whose defaults reference spatial_model_features and monolingual_pk_trigger_model. This ties the option to the language/decoder pipeline.

What KLP can and cannot mean

The APK also contains DelightKlpDownloader, klp_locales, klp_versions, and a setting to load a key-correction model from KLP. Download paths under dl.google.com/gboard/klp/ contain speech and TensorFlow Lite language-model resources. That argues against reducing KLP to keyboard geometry alone. We have not established what KLP stands for, whether a V1 fallback is invoked, or any speed/RAM improvement.

Frequently asked questions

What is the APK default?

False in the decompiled flag declaration. The effective value can be overridden by other configuration.

Does enabling the disable flag select a V1 parser?

That interpretation has not been proven by the identified consumer; the observable code sets configuration fields.

  • Google Research — touch and decoder model context

Independent Gboard field guide | People comparing voice typing behavior

Gboard Voice Typing Flags: Dictation, Commands and Language Support

Learn which Gboard voice typing controls affect UI entry points, dictation models and locale support, and which are still experiments.

What you should know

A voice typing switch can expose a microphone button without proving its speech backend is installed or eligible.

Evidence standard: these are real catalog identifiers, but their effects can be inferred, version-specific, or gated. Check the confidence and APK notes before changing settings.

Begin with the supported microphone path

Gboard includes a standard voice input UI with language and device limitations. Advanced voice typing can have additional eligibility and speech features. First test the normal microphone, punctuation behavior, and chosen language using documented Gboard settings. A modifier flag is meaningful only relative to a working baseline.

What the Atlas flags describe

enable_ondevice_voice suggests a path for local recognition, while enable_global_direct_to_voice_toolbar concerns access to the voice UI. enable_voice_in_japanese indicates language-specific eligibility. enable_agentic_dictation is a separate advanced behavior name; do not infer it is available merely from the identifier. The data path, UI entry point and model-download requirement may all be separate gates.

How to compare without false positives

Read a short fixed phrase, an address and a sentence with punctuation into the same app in similar noise conditions. Record word substitutions, auto-punctuation, microphone source and whether connectivity changes behavior. Keep a note of the exact Gboard build. Never enable diagnostics that record speech content just to test a button.

Frequently asked questions

Does 'on-device' mean Gboard never connects to a server?

Not by itself. It names a potential processing path, not a complete network/privacy audit.

Why is a microphone option missing?

Language, rollout, build, permissions and backend availability can all affect it.

How to Verify Whether a Gboard Flag Really Works

Design a controlled before-and-after test for experimental Gboard features without mistaking visibility for functionality.

What you should know

A good finding pairs the exact APK/build, actual observed behavior, and a repeatable test that isolates one variable.

Evidence standard: these are real catalog identifiers, but their effects can be inferred, version-specific, or gated. Check the confidence and APK notes before changing settings.

Make the claim testable

Replace broad statements like 'makes typing faster' with an observable prediction: for example, a particular UI control appears, or a named suggestion chip becomes available in a defined text field. Write down keyboard version, language, Android version, relevant model downloads, app under test and whether a restart occurred.

Separate code evidence from runtime evidence

Finding a string in DEX proves presence. Identifying an option declaration can reveal its declared default and type. Finding a call site tells us how a value is consumed. None of those alone prove the current effective Phenotype or server-provided value or that a feature changes under normal conditions.

Compare outcomes and document failures

Use the same typing phrase or interaction in both conditions, with one switch changed. Try more than once, include a negative result, and restore the original value. A feature may be gated by locale, account cohort, model availability or patch implementation. Submit the outcome with caveats instead of promoting one lucky observation into a universal claim.

Frequently asked questions

Is decompiling enough for Verified status?

Not for an end-user effect. It can validate a configuration path and type but not a measured on-device outcome.

Can an A/B test override my choice?

Depending on the flag, server-managed values or eligibility may affect what the user sees.

  • Google research on personalized keyboard models

How to Use the GboardWu Flag Editor Without Guesswork

A practical workflow for looking up GboardWu flags, comparing types and defaults, recording changes, and reversing experiments.

What you should know

Search the exact name, inspect the actual editable type, and keep a before/after record before touching an experiment.

Evidence standard: these are real catalog identifiers, but their effects can be inferred, version-specific, or gated. Check the confidence and APK notes before changing settings.

Find the right editor

In a supported GboardWu patch build, look for Patches → More settings → Developer options → Flag Editor. The exact menus may vary by patch version. A normal stock Gboard installation does not expose this workflow. The Atlas is a reference: clicking Copy name copies an identifier; it does not silently change your keyboard.

Don't assume every value is Boolean

Some entries are numeric limits, model names or stored strings rather than switches. Confirm the type and current value displayed in the editor before editing. If a supposed flag is missing, there may be a build mismatch, a removed implementation or a name that was collected from code but not exposed to the editor.

Test and roll back deliberately

Record the version, exact flag name and original value, then perform one change. Some settings require restarting the keyboard to reload its configuration; others require a resource or server-side entitlement that a restart cannot provide. The patch project documents backup/restore of settings and flag-store files, but restore support depends on your installed patch.

Frequently asked questions

Does the Atlas toggle flags?

No. It is a static, searchable index. Changes happen inside whatever compatible editor you choose.

Should I enable every attractive feature?

No. Test isolated, reversible changes only when you can observe a specific result.

How to use this atlas

  1. Search for a feature or browse a category.
  2. Open details to see the exact identifier and what is—and isn't—verified.
  3. Use Copy to paste a name into GboardWu → Patches → More settings → Developer options → Flag Editor.
  4. Change one setting at a time. Some changes require restarting Gboard; many experiments simply won't work on every version.

Why the caution labels?

A string inside an APK isn't proof that a feature is enabled, editable, safe, or available on your device. This catalog separates name-based interpretation from more specific research. Flags linked to AI models, networks, or audio may consume resources or affect privacy.
